body_text: Somewhere between the invention of the internet and the rise of Wi-Fi, someone decided pigeons might be useful again. Back in 2001, Norwegian tech enthusiasts experimented with transmitting internet data via carrier pigeons. Of the nine packets sent, only four replies came back. Not exactly a technological breakthrough. But 25 years later, one of those packets is up for auction at Christie's , with bidding already reaching $4,000. Apparently, even a failed technology venture can appreciate in value. Stocks slid on Tuesday as US crude oil prices ticked higher while the global benchmark dropped. Bumble, the long-struggling dating app, has spent the past five years looking for love in a hopeless place: the Nasdaq stock exchange. The company announced Tuesday that Ithaca Holdings , an investment firm founded by two Silicon Valley veterans that appears to be less than a year old, has agreed to buy it for $1.3 billion cash in a take-private deal. Shareholders will receive $6.05 per share, a whopping 138% premium to Friday's closing price, the last trading day before the Wall Street Journal reported Bumble and Ithaca were in advanced talks. The $1.3 billion price tag may sound like a lot until you remember the company had a peak valuation of about $14 billion around the time it went public in 2021. Bumble has seen its sales decline for the past few years and is expected to report a $15 million net loss for this fiscal year which would mark its fifth consecutive year in the red. It’s unclear exactly how Ithaca plans to turn it around. In a statement, Bumble CEO Whitney Wolfe Herd (who, notably, recused herself from the board vote on the takeover) said Ithaca is “a partner who shares our vision, believes in our women-first mission, and is committed to investing in Bumble’s future.” In case you forgot: Wolfe Herd founded Bumble as a women-focused dating app in 2014, she announced she was stepping down as CEO in 2023, then returned in 2025. Bumble — not unlike its peer apps owned by Match Group — has struggled to keep users engaged, particularly younger ones who are growing tired of endless swiping. Its paying user base shrank 16% year-over-year to 3.2 million in the second quarter , while revenue fell about 15%. The company has been trying to reinvent itself, loosening its signature women-make-the-first-move rule and experimenting with in-person events where users meet before matching. Its biggest planned change is doing away with the swipe altogether, although it hasn't revealed what will replace it. The new model is expected to begin rolling out in early 2027, following technical delays. The takeover also means a changing of the guard: Ithaca founders Ravi Gupta, a former Instacart executive, and John Hegeman, a former Meta executive, will become Bumble's co-CEOs. Wolfe Herd will remain involved with the company she founded. You need a big enough pool of people on your platform. Then you have to convince enough of those people to pay for premium features. And then, if those premium features actually work, you’re perpetually cannibalizing your own subscriber base. Not to mention the tides are turning away from swipe-based apps. title: ⛽ A diesel deal
body_text: Seven masked thieves pulled off an audacious heist at Tuscan warehouse, expertly disabling the alarm system before carting away 30,000 bottles of rare wine, the Financial Times reports . The wine, made by family owned Marchesi Antinori, which traces its history back to 1385, sell from between about $170 and $560 a bottle. The thieves seemed to have intimate knowledge of the specialized storage facility’s operations, with the robbery timed just before Antinori was about to send out consignment shipments to some of its best customers, ensuring the warehouse would be laden with valuable bottles. It’s the most recent in a string of thefts in Italy targeting high-end wine in storage or at restaurant cellars. Antinori says it went public with the sale in the hope that enterprising oenophiles can be on the lookout for the looted bottles. When we last checked in on the White House’s attempts to get the price of diesel down, the President was floating the idea of allowing red dye diesel – which is chemically identical to normal diesel but with added red dye and is exempt from federal taxes but restricted to off-road vehicles – to be used for to be used for normal on-road uses. Energy experts doubted the policy change would do much to push prices downward, and would likely result in red dye diesel becoming more expensive, putting even greater cost pressure on farmers. Now, the White House is trying a different approach: get Russia back into the (legal) petroleum products exports business. On Friday, the Trump administration announced that the US will buy 36 million barrels of Russian diesel over the next several months, with 2.25 million barrels purchased immediately. Prices did initially tick down on the news, but the challenge is the context: the world uses around 30 million barrels of diesel per day. US truckers use almost 3 million barrels of diesel a day, Reuters reports . The news agency pointed out that the shipments of Russian diesel that the US has announced a schedule for thus far amount to less than four days of what US trucks use daily. The Financial Times noted that industry analysts expected the deal to have very little impact on global supplies and thus prices. President Trump went further on Sunday evening, announcing a so-called energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in which both nations would abstain from attacking energy infrastructure. Shortly after the announcement, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia carried out a target strike in violation of the ceasefire. Both the international and US benchmarks for crude oil prices rose a little over 2% on Monday. Attempting to use Russian imports to drive down diesel prices is a tenuous tactic given the scale of the shipments announced thus far, and, as Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid told the FT, the uncertainty of any truce between the Kremlin and Ukraine. But as long as diesel prices stay elevated, expect more policy activity from the White House. “There is a lot of impetus to do more,” Citigroup ’s head of energy strategy Anthony Yuen pointed out , because GOP districts “tend to consume more diesel”. title: 🍿 Comic Con shows what’s next for the entertainment industry
body_text: It happens to all of us: our team is getting smoked on national television. That happens to all of us, right? No matter, but maybe you just want to look away from the game where your quarterback can’t hit a pass for his life, the coach seems as perplexed as you are, and maybe you wince as Cam Skattebo continues to possess the self-preservation instincts of a lit firework. So, you look at your Instagram or something. Well, guess what: advertisers apparently saw that coming. Genius Sports , a UK-data company, has developed a complex map of 250 million American sports fans and collaborates with brands — food delivery companies are a particular favorite, as people tend to notice their own hunger when their team is not sufficiently distracting them — to serve up ads to fans of teams that are losing at especially distraction-prone moments. Apparently one of the major delivery companies sees a 20% uplift in prices when a fan’s team is losing. Stocks rose on Friday as the US struck a deal with Russia to release diesel to international markets helped ease crude prices. Last week saw a number of shifts in the entertainment industry, the largest of which was the long-sought merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. into Skydance , but also saw Netflix indicating that it was weighing layoffs , and Disney indicating it may directly take on Imax . At a glance, the fortunes of the entertainment sector appear to be shifting rapidly, with the future of it relatively cloudy. Last week, though, New York Comic Con offered insight into the future of the industry and intriguing clues as to why the entertainment properties that draw the most eyeballs are increasingly rarely coming from boardrooms in Los Angeles. Remember, entertainment companies are not structured to make money from new ideas. They are companies designed to extract continuous, multifaceted value from ideas they already own. Disney is the archetype of this. Making $12 from a movie ticket is nice, but once the customer is sufficiently entranced by the character, they make $30 from the Halloween costume, $20 from the doll sale, $10 a month from the Disney+ subscription to rewatch the movie, a thousand or more from the cruise and Disney World trip, $80 for the Broadway show ticket, and so on. Historically generating new ideas was done through internal R&D (like making a new movie or character) but lately these companies have been more content to acquire R&D from other, smaller shops. Disney buying Lucasfilm or Marvel fits this model. Amazon Prime’s two biggest shows, “The Boys” and “Invincible,” each raiding the independent press section of the comic shop is another. You can also see how the failure to make a property sufficiently exploitable can cause a problem. Take Netflix; on one hand, they certainly made some ancillary money from its demogorgon stuffies and Broadway show, but “Stranger Things” won’t be stuffing a lot of stockings this year despite the enormous IP investment. On the other hand, “KPop Demon Hunters,” which they bought off Sony, stands to be like every third Halloween costume this year. NYCC is illuminating because it shows the sources of original and speculative R&D on the rise, what’s resonating with audiences, and what’s going to sui generis pop , revealing which fast-growing franchises will be the next Marvel, the The Walking Dead, the next Romantasy to highlight three franchises that were big at NYCC well before becoming billion-dollar grossers for these large content exploitation companies. Dan Buckley, the publisher at Marvel, spoke candidly at the ICV2 Insider Talks panel about why comics have historically been of interest to these large companies: it is a relatively capital- un intensive business. Basically, you can make a comic and if it fails, no biggie. This same is true of books, manga, webtoons, really any situation where you’re paying one creator and shipping cheap pixels or dead trees. It’s not the case with a $200 million movie. If there was a star of this year’s NYCC, it’s likely “Dungeon Crawler Carl” scribe Dan Dinnamman , whose books have been a breakout hit of the emerging LitRPG genre; Comcast snagged the rights for that, which is developing a show for Peacock. For that matter, books, comics, and manga in general: per the ICV2 White Paper presentation, graphic novel sales are up 28% in the first half of 2026, and manga sales are up 39.5% in the book channel; it should not come as a surprise that Netflix (with “One Piece”) and Sony (through Crunchyroll) are pushing manga adaptations. Realistically, breakout IP hits are what define the long-term success of these megacompanies and will define their businesses for the coming years far more than any corporate structure. You make lots of cheap bets and one of them resonates with audiences at which point you can roll it into your lucrative (though capital-intensive) businesses, like cruises and theme parks. Sure, there is fear, uncertainty and doubt about the Warner-Paramount merger within the industry, but its success or failure will likely be defined less by how efficiently they can exploit existing IP — like the announced GI Joe and Transformers adaptations, which I’m certain will be incredibly culturally relevant when they eventually come out — but rather if they make savvy decisions about what new material to buy up. One deal in particular announced last week is intriguing for the future of where these companies are going to source the next generation of stories, and it’s not two dessicated cable companies casting their lots together. Marvel announced a few new projects to compete for new readers, including book publication formats that imitate the smash-hit DC Compact Comics, which in turn imitate the overwhelmingly popular manga book format. But the big one is that after years of unsuccessfully attempting to win over mobile phone-using audiences, Marvel has cut a deal with Webtoon , which dominates the category, to launch its Marvel Comics by Webtoon app .
